title: The Long Road to Mathematical Induction
explainer: The reasoning pattern behind induction appears in fragments long before it had a name or a formal justification — in Euclid's proof that there are infinitely many primes and in techniques used by the 11th-century mathematician al-Karaji. The Italian mathematician Francesco Maurolico gave an early rigorous version in 1575, Blaise Pascal stated it more explicitly in his 1665 treatise on the arithmetical triangle, and it was only pinned down as a formal axiom of arithmetic by 19th-century mathematicians, including Giuseppe Peano and Richard Dedekind. The tool you use to prove a recursive algorithm correct took over two thousand years to become a precise, agreed-upon method.

title: Pascal's Triangle Is Centuries Older Than Pascal
explainer: The triangular array of binomial coefficients central to combinatorics was described in India by around the 10th-11th century, developed independently in Persia (where it's still called the Khayyam triangle, via al-Karaji and Omar Khayyam), and recorded in China by Jia Xian in the 11th century and popularized by Yang Hui in the 13th — all well before Blaise Pascal's 1600s treatise gave it the name used in the West. It's a clean example of the same combinatorial structure being found independently in multiple civilizations, because the underlying mathematics is universal, not culturally specific.
